catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-1.explanation: BMan: Sure, your students will think you’re crazy if you talk about Maths as if it were a spectator sport, but in the end your attitude will rub off on them.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-2.explanation: BWoman: I was reading about some techniques I could try in the classroom to keep their interest levels up.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-3.explanation: BSam: But does that matter, if the music’s brilliant? And it certainly was. But that’s just my opinion.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-4.explanation: ASam: Well – she’s a student – studying comparative literature I think. That seems to give a bit of substance to her music, make it thoughtful and rigorous.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-5.explanation: AWoman: Yes – very convenient. We’re really keen on the idea that the company should be seen to identify with a certain set of values – and I think we were doing just that out there in the woods.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-6.explanation: BWoman: And word seems to have got round because the last bunch of job applicants were a very noticeably higher calibre than previously- and I’m pretty sure that wasn’t just a coincidence, though it wasn’t part of our original thinking.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-7.explanation: queenTermites are like large ants and build amazingly complex structures called mounds to live in. Unlike bees, termites don’t receive instructions from their queen about what to do.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-8.explanation: colonyThis tells us that large numbers of units working independently can, paradoxically, build complicated, large-scale things together. So, we decided to make and to program what I like to call a colony of robots.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-9.explanation: woodOne deposits some soil, for example, or half-eaten wood…another one comes along later and on seeing this, a reaction is triggered.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-10.explanation: (enough) feedbackRather than trying to prevent those errors, we give them enough feedback to help with the recognition and correction process...

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-11.explanation: staircaseI’ve demonstrated this in action several times in public presentations, with one of our robots. It had to try to complete the structure I asked it to, in this case a staircase.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-12.explanation: sandbags/sand bags/ bags of sandSo, for instance, if you wanted to position sandbags to protect against rising floodwater, or build in difficult Antarctic surroundings, you can imagine how hardware and approaches very much like this could be used.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-13.explanation: intelligenceIn a sense, termites are like cells in your brain, all acting independently but interacting with each other, and out of that comes a higher intelligence.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-14.explanation: (mathematical) modelA Turkish group has been working alongside us to see if the way the robots and termites operate can actually be captured in a mathematical model to be used in future projects.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-15.explanation: BMark: Well, we tend to think that all modern problems were invented by us. But actually the 19th century also had traffic problems.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-16.explanation: AJudith:But amazingly, they were started in 1860 and completed by 1863. You wouldn’t expect to finish a single metro line in that time these days.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-17.explanation: DMark: In fact, on the day it opened, an incredible 30,000 people used the railway and the trains were completely full.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-18.explanation: BJudith: And it was a great source of national pride. It’s hard to overestimate its importance in the way London grew – the city actually followed the spread of the underground lines, not the other way round.Mark: And yes, I would say that the Underground really helped create London. The lines spread out towards what were little villages at the time – and are now important areas of the city.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-19.explanation: DJudith: They were deliberately designed as big, cavernous places with an adventurous feel of going underground, massive escalators going everywhere, a bit like the 1920s film Metropolis where you get the sense of being in a really huge city with lots of people going different places.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-20.explanation: AMark: I think that’s one of the main ways it became something in people’s heads as a system, as an icon, of London.

I wandered into the town centre and saw the museum, and I remembered how my mother always used to say that local museums are often a mine of information

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-26.explanation: BThere was plenty of material, well displayed – and a temporary exhibition of deep-sea fishing equipment – but more importantly all the stuff was closely associated with the town, and reflected its history as a once thriving fishing port.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-27.explanation: CSo to fill the time, I tried out one of those tape machines and listened to a lively commentary which certainly made the displays and reconstructions more relevant.

catalog-listening-cae-c1-test14-q-29.explanation: HAnd to crown it all – instead of having everything in cabinets, they’ve built mock-up scenes – like a medieval kitchen for example – convincingly realistic and much more effective.
